title: Here I Am: New Heavens and a New Earth
summary: God answers the people's prayer. He has been reaching out all day to a rebellious people who practice forbidden rites, and he will repay them, but he will not destroy the whole cluster: his servants will inherit the land. The chapter divides the future of the faithful from that of the rebels and ends with God creating new heavens and a new earth, a Jerusalem of joy where no one weeps, labor is not wasted, and the wolf and the lamb feed together.
story: In 63:7 to 64:12 the people asked why God was silent and hidden. Chapter 65 is his reply, and it turns the question around: God has not been hiding. He has been saying Here I am to people who did not seek him and holding out his hands to people who refused him. The chapter then does something the lament did not expect. It separates Israel into two groups, the servants and the rebels, and gives them opposite futures. That division runs through the last chapters of Isaiah and prepares for the book's final scene in chapter 66. The vision of new heavens and a new earth in verses 17 to 25 is one of the Bible's great horizons, picked up again at the close of the whole Bible in Revelation 21.
historical:
The practices condemned in verses 3 to 7 and 11 fit the religious life of Judah both before the exile and among those who remained in or returned to the land afterward, and scholars date the chapter accordingly: many place it in the late sixth or early fifth century BC among the returned community, while those who hold to a single author read it as Isaiah's prophecy of a divided people to come. The chapter's sharp line between God's servants and those who forsake him may reflect real tensions in postexilic Judah, where groups disagreed over worship and who belonged to the true Israel, tensions also visible in Ezra, Nehemiah, and Malachi.

The place names in verse 10 frame the whole land. The Sharon is the fertile coastal plain on the west, and the Valley of Achor lies near Jericho on the east, the place where Achan was stoned after the fall of Jericho (Joshua 7:24-26). Hosea had already promised that the Valley of Achor would become a door of hope (Hosea 2:15). From sea to Jordan, the land will be pasture again.
cultural:
Verses 3 to 5 describe rites that the law forbade. Sacrificing in gardens points to worship at sacred groves, often linked with fertility religion (compare Isaiah 1:29). Altars of brick broke the command that altars be made of earth or unhewn stone (Exodus 20:24-25). Sitting among graves and spending nights in secret places suggests seeking the dead or seeking dreams from spirits, practices banned in Deuteronomy 18:10-12. Pork and polluted broth broke the food laws of Leviticus 11. And the claim I am holier than you shows people who believed these rites made them specially sacred, so that others must not touch them.

Verse 11 names two gods. Fortune (Gad) was a deity of luck known across the region, and Destiny (Meni) seems to be a god of fate or allotted portion. Setting a table and filling bowls of mixed wine describes a sacred meal offered to them. The next verse makes a pun: those who pour wine for Meni will be destined (Hebrew manah, to number or allot) for the sword. The image of new wine in a cluster (verse 8) comes from the vineyard: a farmer does not destroy a whole bunch of grapes because some are bad, if there is still good juice in it.
literary: The chapter is a divine speech in poetry, built on contrast. Verses 1 to 7 set God's open hands against a people's closed hearts. Verses 8 to 16 alternate between My servants and you in a series of reversals: My servants will eat, but you will go hungry, and so on through drinking, rejoicing, and shouting for joy. Verses 17 to 25 then widen to a whole new creation, echoing earlier passages in Isaiah: the former things will not be remembered (compare 43:18-19), and verse 25 compresses the peaceable kingdom of 11:6-9 into a single line, adding that the serpent's food will be dust, a clear echo of the curse in Genesis 3:14. The new creation undoes the old curses one by one: early death, work stolen by others, children born to disaster, prayers unheard.

outline.t: God's outstretched hands and a rebellious people
A blessing kept in the cluster: the servants inherit
Two destinies: servants and those who forsake the LORD
New heavens, new earth, and a joyful Jerusalem

doctrines.note: God speaks of creating new heavens and a new earth with the same verb used in Genesis 1:1. The future he promises is not an escape from the created world but its renewal: houses, vineyards, long lives, children, and animals at peace.

The chapter gives God's people a concrete hope: no more weeping, no wasted work, no early death, answered prayer. It is the Old Testament's fullest picture of the world to come, and the New Testament builds directly on it.

Idolatry here includes forbidden rites, contact with the dead, and meals for Fortune and Destiny, gods of luck and fate. Trust in chance and fate rather than in the living God is treated as forsaking him.

God will repay the rebels measure for measure, yet he will not destroy all. Judgment separates the faithful from the unfaithful within the same people, which means belonging to Israel by birth does not guarantee sharing in the promise.

words.note: Eved, servant or slave. In Isaiah 40 to 53 the word is almost always singular, the Servant of the LORD who suffers for others. From chapter 54 on it becomes plural: the servants, those who share the Servant's faith and receive his inheritance. The word appears seven times in this chapter and is the name for the faithful remnant.

Bara, to create, the verb reserved for God's own acts and used in Genesis 1:1. It appears three times in verses 17 and 18: God will create new heavens and a new earth, and create Jerusalem to be a joy. The future is presented as a work as fresh and divine as the first creation.

Amen, the word used to confirm that something is true and firm. In verse 16 God is twice called the God of truth, literally the God of Amen: the God whose word is reliable and who keeps what he promises. Revelation 3:14 calls Christ the Amen, the faithful and true witness.

christ: Paul quotes verses 1 and 2 in Romans 10:20-21. He applies verse 1, God found by those who did not seek him, to the Gentiles coming to faith in Christ, and verse 2, God holding out his hands to a disobedient people, to Israel. Isaiah's own context is a word to Israel, and Paul reads it as describing the wider pattern of grace he saw in his own day. The vision of new heavens and a new earth becomes the Christian hope: 2 Peter 3:13 looks for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells, and Revelation 21:1-5 describes a new heaven and new earth, a new Jerusalem, and a God who wipes away every tear, echoing verse 19. The New Testament ties that renewal to Jesus's resurrection, the first piece of the new creation, and to his return. The Servant's servants of this chapter are, for Christians, those who belong to the Servant who suffered and was raised.

hard.q: If there is no more death in the new creation, why does verse 20 speak of people dying at a hundred?
hard.a:
Revelation 21:4 says there will be no more death, yet Isaiah 65:20 says the youth will die at a hundred years and the sinner will be accursed. Readers have taken this in three main ways. Many premillennial interpreters see verses 20 to 25 as describing an earthly thousand-year reign of Christ before the final state (Revelation 20), a time of long life and peace in which death and sin still exist but are greatly restrained. Many amillennial and postmillennial interpreters, along with a large number of Old Testament scholars, read the passage as poetry that describes the unimaginable future in the best terms the prophet's hearers knew: long life, fruitful work, safe children. To say that dying at a hundred would be dying young is a way of saying death will lose its grip, and the New Testament's fuller revelation says it will be abolished. A third view connects the passage primarily to the restoration of Jerusalem after the exile, seen as a foretaste of something greater.

These readings differ on the millennium, a second-order question on which faithful Christians disagree. All agree that the chapter promises a real renewed world, not a disembodied heaven, and that God's intention is to end weeping and wasted life.

questions: God says he held out his hands all day long to people who did not want him. How does that picture of God's patience challenge the way you think about him?
Fortune and Destiny were gods of luck and fate. In what ways do people today still set a table for luck or fate instead of trusting God?
The new creation in verses 17 to 25 includes houses, gardens, work, and children. How does it change your hope to know that God plans to renew this world rather than leave it behind?
